newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's army says government not doing enough.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's army says government not doing enough.

text.p: Zaire's army, battling Tutsi rebels in the east, said on Saturday that the government was not doing enough to help it.
"We regret that the government is moving too slowly and has not yet given us the necessary means," Army Chief of General Staff General Eluki Monga Aundu told a Kinshasa news conference.
Reports from the east suggest that the Zairean army, whose soldiers have a reputation for lack of discipline and looting, is hard-pressed.
Journalists and other sources say the towns of Bukavu and Uvira, where the rebel offensive began two weeks ago, are in rebel hands.
Reports from the main refugee town of Goma say that troops from Tutsi-led neighbour Rwanda were fighting alongside Tutsi rebels there.
Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo, who is part Tutsi and under growing pressure to resign, said on Friday that both towns were in Zairean army hands.
"Nobody can say that the army doesn't have the means for its operations," he told reporters in the capital.
The Zairean army, which has its main base in the east in Goma, is backed by militiamen.
Some reports say Hutu hardliners from the former Rwandan army, who fled to Zaire with over a million fellow Hutus after the 1994 genocide of Tutsis in Rwanda, were also fighting the rebels.
Several hundred protesters in the capital marched to Kengo's offices on Friday and called for his dismissal. Elsewhere, a mob attacked Tutsi-owned shops and looted cars.

Kengo dismissed the criticism. "When a war starts people look for a scapegoat. Today it happens to be the prime minister and his government, but I will continue to work without listening to malicious gossip," he said.
In Brazzaville, capital of neighbouring Congo, representatives of opposition leader Etienne Tshisekedi called for Kengo's arrest, accusing him of complicity with Rwanda.
"We ask the armed forces of Zaire to arrest Kengo immediately for high treason and court martial him," they said in a statement.

Tshisekedi, who claims the job of prime minister which he previously held, is a bitter rival of Kengo, who was appointed in 1994 by the transitional parliament set up as part of Zaire's much-delayed and sometimes bloody democratic transition.

Zaire's veteran president, Mobutu Sese Seko, who seized power and ruled unchallenged until foreign and domestic pressure forced him to embrace democratic reforms in 1990, has been out of the country since August, when he had surgery for prostate cancer in Switzerland.
